page_title: Understanding Your Mobile Plan - Digital Confidence Centre
title: Understanding Your Mobile Plan
description: Figure out what you actually use your phone for, understand mobile data and your bill, compare prepaid and postpaid plans, and negotiate a better deal. Free, plain-language lesson for Canadian seniors. No account needed.
lesson_time: About 30 minutes, at your own pace
lead: Why long-term customers often overpay, how to match a plan to what you actually use, and a simple, polite phone script that can save you $20 to $40 a month.

story.label: Harold's $40 mistake
paragraphs: Harold is 82 years old. He has had the same mobile plan for six years. He pays $85 a month for 2 GB of data plus unlimited talk and text. But when his granddaughter checked his usage, she discovered he only uses about 500 MB of data each month, a quarter of what he pays for.
Harold was overpaying by about $40 every month. That is $480 a year, enough for a weekend trip to see his great-grandchildren.

Here is the thing most people do not realise: your mobile provider will almost never call you to suggest a cheaper plan. Even if a better plan exists, they have no reason to tell you. You are already paying more. That extra money goes straight to their bottom line.

coach: Phone plans change names, prices, and rules constantly. Even people who work in technology struggle to compare them. If choosing a plan feels overwhelming, that is the market being complicated, not you being slow. A few plain questions, which this lesson gives you, cut through almost all of it.

sections.text: There has never been a better time to check

The good news? Canadian cellular prices declined 16.7% between 2023 and 2024. Plans for light users now start at $30 to $45 a month. Prepaid plans for calls and texts only can be as low as $15 to $25 a month. There has never been a better time to review your plan.

sections.label: Why this matters
sections.text: You would not keep paying for a newspaper subscription you do not read. Your mobile plan is the same idea. You deserve a plan that matches what you actually use, not what someone sold you years ago.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: Do you know how much you pay each month for your mobile plan? If not, that is perfectly okay. We will figure it out together in the bill section below.
What do you actually use your phone for?
Before you can pick the right plan, you need to understand how you actually use your phone. Most people overestimate their usage. Here is a simple way to think about it.
Which type of phone user are you?

items: Level 1, Calls only: you mainly make and receive phone calls. You rarely send texts and do not use the internet on your phone. You need a basic talk plan or prepaid plan ($15 to $25/month).
Level 2, Calls + texts: you call and text regularly: family, friends, maybe your doctor's office. You do not browse the internet much on your phone. A talk and text plan is enough ($25 to $35/month).

Level 3, Calls + texts + photos: you call, text, and occasionally send photos to family. You might look up a recipe or check the weather. A light data plan with 1 to 2 GB is right for you ($30 to $45/month).
Level 4, Full usage: you use your phone for email, social media, video calls, maps, streaming, and more. You need a data plan with 4 GB or more ($45 to $65/month).

sections.label: How to check your actual usage
sections.text: On your iPhone, go to Settings, then Cellular. Scroll down to see how much data each app has used. This gives you a clear picture of your real usage. You can also check your monthly usage by logging into your provider's app or website, or by calling them and asking.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: Which level sounds most like you? There is no wrong answer. Knowing your level is the first step to the right plan.
Understanding mobile data

Mobile data is the internet connection your phone uses when you are not connected to Wi-Fi. Everything you do online, checking email, looking at photos, watching videos, uses data. But not all activities use the same amount.
The jar metaphor: what 1 GB looks like
Think of your monthly data as a jar of water. Different activities drink from that jar at very different speeds:

items: Email (text only) = drops from an eyedropper. You could send and receive thousands of emails on 1 GB. Barely makes a dent.
Sending photos = cups of water. Each photo you send by text or email uses a small cup from your jar. A few photos a day is still very manageable.
Browsing the web = glasses of water. Looking up recipes, checking the news, or searching for information uses a moderate amount. An hour of browsing uses roughly 60 MB.
Video calls (FaceTime) = pitchers of water. A 30-minute FaceTime call uses about 400 MB, almost half of 1 GB.
Streaming video (YouTube, Netflix) = buckets of water. One hour of video can use 1 to 3 GB, your entire monthly jar in a single sitting.

sections.label: Wi-Fi does not use your data
sections.text: When you are connected to Wi-Fi, at home, at the library, at a coffee shop, your phone uses that Wi-Fi connection instead of your mobile data. Anything you do on Wi-Fi is free and does not count towards your plan. If you spend most of your time at home on Wi-Fi, you may need very little mobile data.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: Now you know: email uses drops, photos use cups, and video uses buckets. That one idea can save you real money.
Reading your mobile bill

Mobile bills are designed to be confusing. They are often four or five pages long, full of line items that blur together. But once you know what to look for, it becomes much simpler. Every bill breaks down into just four main parts.
The four parts of every mobile bill

items: 1. Your plan cost: the monthly charge for your talk, text, and data plan. It is the core of your bill. Example: $45/month for unlimited talk + text + 2 GB data.

2. Device payment: if you got your phone through your provider on a monthly payment plan, this shows up as a separate line. Example: $15/month for 24 months. Once paid off, this line should disappear. If it does not, call and ask.

3. Extras and add-ons: additional charges for things like voicemail, call display, insurance, or international calling. Many people pay for extras they do not use or did not knowingly add. Review this section carefully.
4. Taxes: HST (13% in Ontario) is added on top of everything. You cannot avoid this, but knowing it is there helps you understand the total.

sections.title: What to look for right now
steps: Pull out your most recent mobile bill (paper or online).
Find any device payment (it may say $0 if your phone is paid off).
Find any extras or add-ons you are being charged for.
Write these three numbers down. You will use them when you call your provider.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: You now know the four parts of your bill. That puts you ahead of most people. Knowledge is power, especially when it saves you money.
Prepaid vs postpaid: what is the difference?
There are two main types of mobile plans in Canada, and understanding the difference can save you a lot of money and stress.
Prepaid: pay first, use after
With a prepaid plan, you pay at the beginning of the month (or buy a set amount of credit). You get a fixed amount of calls, texts, and data. When it runs out, it stops. No surprise charges.

items: Best for: light users who want a predictable, low monthly cost
Typical cost: $15 to $35/month
No credit check required
No contract; stop any time

sections.text: Postpaid: use first, pay after

With a postpaid plan, you use your phone all month and get a bill at the end. This is the most common type of plan in Canada. The risk? If you go over your data limit, you may see extra charges on your bill.

items: Best for: people who use more data and want a consistent service
Typical cost: $40 to $85/month
May include a phone on a payment plan
Overage charges are possible if you exceed your data

sections.label: Which one is right for you?
sections.text: If you are a Level 1 or Level 2 user (calls only, or calls and texts), prepaid is almost always the better deal. You pay less, and there are no surprises. If you are a Level 3 or Level 4 user, postpaid may make more sense, but shop around. The price differences between providers can be $20 or more for the same service.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: Prepaid = pay first, no surprises. Postpaid = pay after, possible overages. That is the whole idea in two sentences.
How to compare plans

Comparing mobile plans used to mean visiting multiple stores and talking to salespeople who each told you their plan was the best. Today, there are free online tools that do the comparing for you, honestly and without trying to sell you anything.

sections.title: Using PlanHub.ca to compare every Canadian provider
steps: Go to PlanHub.ca on your iPad or phone.
Enter your province (Ontario) and choose how much data you need.
It will show you every available plan, sorted by price, cheapest first.

sections.text: PlanHub is a tool, not a store. It does not sell you anything. It just shows you what is available. WhistleOut Canada (whistleout.ca) works similarly: it lets you filter by price, data amount, and provider, and it also shows special promotions that may not be advertised in stores. Both tools are free, Canadian, and designed to help you make an informed choice.

sections.label: Ask a family member for help
sections.text: If using a comparison website feels unfamiliar, ask a family member or trusted friend to sit with you for 10 minutes and look at plans together. You make the decision; they just help navigate the website.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: You do not need to be a tech expert to compare plans. PlanHub.ca and WhistleOut do the hard work for you.
The negotiation call

This is the most empowering part of this lesson. You are going to learn a simple, polite phone script that can save you $20 to $40 a month. You do not need to be confrontational. You do not need to threaten to leave. You just need to ask the right question.
Your plan review script

Call the number on the back of your bill. When you reach a representative, say: "Hello. I have been a customer for [X] years. I'd like to do a plan review. I have looked at my usage and I use less than [X] GB per month. What is the best plan you have for someone who uses less than [X] GB per month?"

That is it. Polite, clear, and informed. The key phrases are "plan review" and "best plan for someone who uses less than". These signal to the representative that you know your usage and are looking for a better deal.
Tips for a successful call

items: Call on a Tuesday or Wednesday morning; wait times are shorter
Have your most recent bill in front of you
Know your average monthly data usage (check Settings, then Cellular on your iPhone)
If the first representative cannot help, politely ask for the "retention" or "loyalty" department; they have access to better deals
Write down what they offer. Say "Thank you, I will think about it" if you are not sure. You do not have to decide on the spot.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: You have every right to ask for a better plan. You are a loyal customer. A polite phone call is all it takes.
Avoiding the upgrade trap

Every year or two, your provider may contact you and suggest it is time to upgrade your phone. They may say things like "Your phone is getting old" or "We have a great new deal on the latest model." This is a sales tactic, not advice.
Your phone probably works fine

Modern smartphones, especially iPhones, are built to last 4 to 6 years or more. If your phone still makes calls, sends texts, takes photos, and runs your apps, there is no reason to replace it. The only reasons to consider a new phone are: the battery no longer holds a charge all day (a battery replacement is much cheaper than a new phone), the phone no longer receives software updates (check Settings, then General, then Software Update), or the screen is cracked and repairs cost more than a replacement.
Unlocked vs locked phones

A locked phone is tied to one provider. It only works with the provider that sold it to you. If you want to switch providers, you may need to get it unlocked first (in Canada, providers must unlock your phone for free upon request). An unlocked phone works with any provider. You can buy one outright from Apple or an electronics store and then choose any plan from any provider. This gives you the most freedom and often saves money in the long run.

sections.label: The real cost of a "free" phone upgrade
sections.text: When a provider offers you a "free" or "$0 down" phone, the cost is hidden in your monthly bill. A phone that costs $0 upfront may add $20 to $35/month to your bill for 24 months. That is $480 to $840 in total. A "free" phone is never truly free.

sections.label: Confidence check
sections.text: Your current phone likely has 2 to 3 more good years in it. Do not let anyone pressure you into an upgrade you do not need.
Quick answers
Will I lose my phone number if I switch providers?

No. In Canada, you have the legal right to keep your phone number when you switch providers. This is called "number portability." Your new provider will handle the transfer for you; just ask them when you sign up.
Is it safe to switch to a smaller provider like Public Mobile or Lucky Mobile?

Yes. In Canada, smaller providers (sometimes called flanker brands) actually use the exact same cell towers as the big providers. Public Mobile and Lucky Mobile use the same network towers. You get the same coverage at a lower price.
What happens if I use more data than my plan includes?

On a prepaid plan, your data simply stops working until the next month, with no extra charges. On a postpaid plan, most Canadian providers now offer "data overage protection" that slows your speed instead of charging extra. Check with your provider to confirm this is turned on for your account.

sections.label: Try it today
sections.text: Check your real data usage: open Settings, then Cellular, and see what you actually use. If it is far below what you pay for, you have everything you need for a plan review call.

sections.heading: Quick check: test your knowledge
sections.intro: Tap the answer you think is correct. There is no score kept and nothing to sign in to.

questions.q: 1. Long-term customers often pay more for mobile plans because:
options: They use more data
Carriers save promotional pricing for new customers and do not automatically lower existing bills
Their phones are older
They have better coverage
questions.right: Correct. Providers have no reason to volunteer a cheaper plan to an existing customer. That is exactly how Harold ended up overpaying $40 a month for six years.
questions.wrong: The real reason is that carriers save their best pricing for new customers and never automatically lower an existing bill. You have to ask, like Harold's plan review.

options: You use your phone at home during peak hours
You use your phone outside your carrier's coverage area, especially internationally
You use too much data in one month
You call numbers in other provinces
questions.right: Right. Roaming means your phone is using another network outside your carrier's coverage area, most often when travelling internationally, and that costs extra.
questions.wrong: Roaming charges happen when you use your phone outside your carrier's coverage area, especially internationally. Calls within Canada on your own network are not roaming.

questions.q: 3. To avoid unexpected roaming charges when travelling internationally, you should:
options: Turn off data roaming in settings or get a travel add-on before you leave
Only make calls, not use data
Switch to a new carrier when you land
Only use your phone on Wi-Fi and disable calls
questions.right: Exactly. Turning off data roaming in your settings, or buying a travel add-on before you leave, prevents surprise charges from the moment you land.
questions.wrong: The reliable protection is to turn off data roaming in your settings or arrange a travel add-on before you leave. Calls can roam too, so limiting data alone is not enough.

questions.q: 4. Budget mobile carriers often offer lower prices because:
options: Their coverage is always worse than the big three
They operate on the same networks as major carriers but with less overhead and marketing
They do not comply with CRTC regulations
They limit calls to local numbers only
questions.right: Correct. Flanker brands like Public Mobile and Lucky Mobile use the exact same towers as the big providers. Same coverage, lower price.
questions.wrong: Budget carriers run on the same networks as the major carriers; they just spend less on overhead and marketing. Coverage is the same, and they follow the same CRTC rules.

options: Getting a new phone number when you switch carriers
Keeping your existing phone number when switching to a new carrier
Transferring contacts to a new phone
Forwarding calls from one number to another
questions.right: Right. In Canada you have the legal right to keep your phone number when you switch providers. Your new provider handles the transfer.
questions.wrong: Number porting is keeping your existing phone number when you switch to a new carrier. It is your legal right in Canada, and the new provider does the work.

sections.heading: Your progress
sections.intro: Tick each item as you feel confident with it. This is saved on this device only, with no account needed.
items: I know which usage level I am (calls only, calls + texts, light data, or full usage)
I have checked my real data usage in Settings, then Cellular
I can find the four parts of my mobile bill: plan, device payment, extras, taxes
I understand the difference between prepaid and postpaid plans
I have compared plans on PlanHub.ca or WhistleOut Canada
I know the plan review script for calling my provider
I know a "free" phone upgrade is never truly free

success_state: Well done. You know what you actually use your phone for, how to read your bill, and how to ask for a plan review in one polite call. That is how Harold's $40 mistake stops happening to you.
